# Figure 3 — The period-3 positional carrier supports donor–acceptor routing

**Generated by** `scripts/splicebert/make_fig3_clock_circuit.py` from
`results/phase-lattice/fig_report_data.json`. Model: **SpliceBERT.1024nt**.

This is the causal figure. Everything else in the report describes structure; this shows that
removing the structure breaks the behaviour, and that putting one head back repairs it.

## A — Each comb head reads one carrier phase, and it *chooses* which

Six heads, six weight-only positional responses R(k). Each is a comb with period 3, and each
locks to **one carrier phase** (highlighted teeth). The phase wheel shows why: a head's phase
preference is the rotation angle its QK bilinear form induces on the carrier plane, predicted in
closed form as `atan2(−Qs, Pc)` with no fitting to R(k) at all.

Predicted versus measured, worst case across all six heads: **0.76°**, against **120°** between
phase classes. The heads do not read a phase label off the table. They
select one, and we can predict which from the weights alone.

## B — Only the carrier's own band matters

Phase mass per head, under three conditions. Deleting the **period-3 band** drives every comb to
**chance (1/3)**. Deleting an **energy-matched control band** leaves them essentially untouched.
The effect is not "perturbing the table hurts things" — it is specific to the seven bins that
carry the positional signal.

## C — Coupling collapses first, and fastest

Attenuating the carrier by a factor α and measuring three outcomes, each normalised to the
headroom it had when intact. At **full deletion (α = 0)**:

| Outcome | Headroom kept |
|---|---|
| Intron prediction | **82%** — barely touched |
| Exon prediction | **32%** |
| **Donor–acceptor coupling** | **3%** — gone |

Full deletion affects the three readouts differently and almost eliminates donor–acceptor coupling,
while the energy-matched control band leaves the dose curves largely unchanged. Because the full-lesion
health gate fails and the runner's exon label was not annotation-derived, this panel is supportive
dose/control evidence, not evidence of coding specificity or reading-frame sensing.

## D — Comparative mediation, against **size-matched** nulls

This panel is scored carefully, and the care changes what it says.

The random-head controls come in **two sizes**, and pooling them would have been a category
error:

- **24 one-head nulls** — restoring a single random head. They top out at **4.2%**.
- **24 six-head nulls** — restoring six random heads. Median 6.3%, but the maximum is **93.9%**.

So: L2H15 alone recovers **36.3%** of the lost coupling, and L3H1 **34.8%** — each roughly **8×
the best of 24 random single heads** (exact add-one p = 0.040, the floor at 24 nulls). That is a
strong, specific, comparative claim.

But **all six combs together recover 96.3%, and one random six-head set recovered 93.9%.** The
six-head result is *not* comfortably outside its own null, and the figure draws that tail rather
than hiding it. Restoring six of ninety-six heads is simply a large intervention; the honest
reading is that the *single-head* comparisons carry the mediation claim and the six-head one does
not add much.

**"All 16 layer-2 heads" has no size-matched null at all.** It is drawn greyed out and labelled
"no matched null" rather than being silently compared against the wrong distribution. It is
reported; it is not evidence.

## Two runs, two baselines — not mixed

Panel C is the **dose** run (n = 256): coupling 0.946 → 0.026. Panel D is the **mediation** run
(n = 160), which has its own baseline, 0.943 → 0.034; its percentages are of *that* lost
coupling. These are separate experiments and the figure keeps them separate.
